TÃ³rshavn, meaning "Thor's harbour" in Faroese and named after the Norse god of thunder, is the capital and largest municipality of the Faroe Islands, a self-governing dependency within the Kingdom of Denmark situated in the North Atlantic Ocean between Iceland and Norway.[1][2] Located on the southeastern coast of Streymoy, the archipelago's principal island, TÃ³rshavn has served since the 9th century as the site for the annual assembly of the LÃ¸gting, the Faroese parliament recognized as among the world's oldest continuously functioning legislatures.[3]The municipality, which includes adjacent settlements such as HoyvÃk and Argir, had a population of approximately 23,000 in 2023, comprising nearly half of the Faroe Islands' total inhabitants of 54,149.[4][5] As the political, administrative, and economic hub of the islands, TÃ³rshavn hosts key institutions including government offices on the historic Tinganes peninsula, features a deep-water harbor central to fishing and trade, and supports a growing tourism sector alongside services and light industry.[6][7] Its blend of traditional turf-roofed wooden houses in the old town with modern infrastructure underscores its evolution from a Viking-era trading post to a resilient Nordic urban center adapted to subarctic conditions.[8]
Geography
Location and topography
TÃ³rshavn lies at coordinates 62Â°01â²N 6Â°46â²W on the southeastern coast of Streymoy, the largest and most populous island in the Faroe Islands archipelago, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.[9][10] This positioning in a natural harbor has historically facilitated its role as the archipelago's primary port and administrative center, despite the islands' remote North Atlantic location approximately 400 kilometers northwest of Scotland.[11][12]The topography features a sheltered bay enclosed by steep hills and rugged terrain typical of basaltic volcanic origins, with elevations rising quickly from sea level to over 300 meters nearby.[13] Limited flat land along the waterfront constrains urban expansion, resulting in a dense, compact settlement pattern integrated into the fjord-like inlet and surrounding slopes.[14] The area's vulnerability to coastal erosion and landslides stems from thin soil layers over rocky substrates, influencing infrastructure development and land use.[15]As the de facto capital, TÃ³rshavn's urban area extends continuously into adjacent villages, incorporating HoyvÃk to the north and Argir to the south, forming a metropolitan zone amid Streymoy's varied coastal and inland features.[10][16] This integration reflects the practical constraints of the island's elongated, mountainous profile, which spans about 50 kilometers north-south with narrow valleys and high plateaus limiting large-scale sprawl.[17]
Climate and environment
TÃ³rshavn features a subpolar oceanic climate (KÃ¶ppen Cfc), moderated by the North Atlantic Current, which prevents extreme cold despite its high latitude. Average temperatures range from 3.5Â°C in January to 10.5Â°C in July, with annual means around 6.8Â°C based on long-term observations from local meteorological stations. Winters are mild but persistently damp and windy, while summers remain cool and overcast, with rare exceedances above 15Â°C. Precipitation totals approximately 1,300 mm annually, distributed evenly throughout the year, often as fine drizzle or mist, contributing to over 200 rainy days per year. Winds, predominantly westerly, average 8-10 m/s, with gusts frequently exceeding 20 m/s due to the islands' exposure in the North Atlantic.[18][19]The environmental conditions support limited terrestrial biodiversity, dominated by grasses, mosses, and low shrubs adapted to constant moisture and wind; higher plants are scarce, with only about 400 native vascular plant species recorded across the Faroe Islands. Seabird populations thrive in coastal areas, but inland ecosystems reflect the archipelago's post-glacial origins, with sheep grazing exerting significant pressure on vegetation cover. The short growing season, constrained to roughly May through September with fewer than 1,000 growing degree days annually, restricts agriculture to marginal potato and grass cultivation on less than 4% of land suitable for farming, fostering heavy dependence on imported foodstuffs and reinforcing the fishing sector's economic primacy.[20][21][22]Human adaptations to the harsh weather include traditional turf-roofed structures, which utilize layered grass and peat for superior thermal insulationâretaining heat in winter and cooling in brief summersâwhile blending with the landscape and aiding water runoff in heavy rains. Modern buildings incorporate similar green roofing principles alongside oil-fired heating systems to combat persistent humidity and wind chill, ensuring habitability without reliance on extreme measures. These practices stem from centuries of empirical necessity rather than aesthetic preference, as evidenced by their persistence in both rural and urban settings.[23][24][25]
History
Early settlement and Viking era
The Norse colonization of the Faroe Islands commenced in the 9th century, building on sparse pre-Norse human activity evidenced by sedimentary ancient DNA and fecal biomarkers indicating livestock introduction (sheep and possibly cattle) and barley processing around 500 CE, likely by transient Celtic hermits or explorers rather than permanent settlers.[26] Traditional accounts, drawn from the FÃ¦reyinga Saga, attribute the initial organized Norse landnÃ¡m (settlement) to GrÃmur Kamban circa 825 CE, a figure with possible Celtic ties from the Hebrides or Ireland, reflecting migration patterns from overpopulated Scandinavian and peripheral Norse communities seeking arable land and fishing grounds amid Atlantic expansion.[27] Archaeological radiocarbon dating from sites across the islands corroborates this timeframe, with Viking Age farms appearing from the late 8th to 9th centuries, supplanting any ephemeral prior occupation through sustained agrarian and maritime adaptation.[28]TÃ³rshavn's origins trace to this Norse influx, its name denoting "Thor's Harbor" in testament to pagan settler priorities, with the Tinganes peninsula emerging as the locus for the LÃ¸gtingâthe regional thing assembly for dispute resolution, law-making, and chieftain gatheringsâestablished in the Viking Age, traditionally around 825 CE though archaeological confirmation centers on 9th-10th century activity.[29] This site's selection stemmed from its defensible rocky promontory dividing a natural deep-water harbor, facilitating periodic influxes for assemblies while permanent habitation remained limited to scattered farmsteads, as evidenced by excavations on nearby Streymoy such as NiÃ°ri Ã¡ Toft in KvÃvÃk, yielding longhouse remains and artifacts from the Viking Period.[28] The assembly's role underscores causal drivers of settlement: not mythic conquest but pragmatic centralization of authority in a dispersed, kin-based society navigating isolation.Economically, early TÃ³rshavn functioned as a modest nodal point for intra-island exchange and limited overseas links, with paleoeconomic data from regional sites revealing self-reliant subsistence via dominant sheep herding (providing wool and meat), supplementary cattle and pig husbandry, marine fishing, seabird exploitation, and marginal barley farming constrained by the subarctic climate.[28]Trade causation arose from resource complementarity, importing essentials like steatite querns and vessels from Norway and grindstones from the British Isles, bartered for local wool, hides, and preserved fishâthough walrus ivory, prized in broader Viking networks, played minimal role here due to scarce northern access.[28]Population density stayed low, with island-wide estimates implying tiny clusters under a hundred at key sites like TÃ³rshavn by 1000 CE, prioritizing resilience over expansion amid environmental limits and pre-industrial transport constraints.[30] Pagan practices persisted through the era, with Christian transition evident only later via imported influences, laying groundwork for sites like foundational church structures without abrupt cultural overwrite.[28]
Medieval to early modern period (1500â1800)
Following Norway's entry into the Kalmar Union in 1380, the Faroe Islands, including TÃ³rshavn, fell under the joint Danish-Norwegian realm, with de facto Danish dominance solidifying after the union's dissolution in 1523. TÃ³rshavn emerged as the primary administrative hub, housing royal bailiffs and officials who collected tithes and enforced crown policies amid feudal structures that prioritized Copenhagen's interests over local prosperity.[31]In 1580, local magnate Magnus Heinason erected the Skansin fortress overlooking the harbor to counter persistent pirate threats, marking an early effort to secure the settlement's role in limited trade activities. By 1584, TÃ³rshavn's population numbered just 101, evenly split among farming households and servants, administrative and trading personnel, and craftsmen, reflecting a stagnant economy tethered to Danish mercantilism.[32][33]The Danish royal trade monopoly, entrenching exclusive exchanges via crown-sanctioned ships, suppressed independent commerce and fostered dependency, compelling islanders to remit goods like dried fish and wool while importing essentials at unfavorable terms. This system persisted through the 17th century, exacerbating vulnerabilities during crises and limiting urban growth in TÃ³rshavn.[34]In 1709, the crown revoked the islands' lease to private monopolists such as the Gabel family, reinstating direct governance from Denmark, yet retained the trade restrictions that perpetuated economic extraction. Early 18th-century epidemics further halved populations in affected areas, underscoring the perils of isolation and poor sanitation, though communities rebounded through intensified reliance on inshore fishing and pastoralism, which provided caloric stability absent broader diversification.[35][36][37]
Industrialization and autonomy (1800âpresent)
The development of the fishing industry marked the onset of industrialization in TÃ³rshavn during the mid-19th century, following the introduction of cod processing techniques by Holger JacobÃ¦us in 1844 and the commencement of deep-sea fishing operations in the harbor by 1872.[38][39] These advancements, coupled with the shift toward commercial fisheries after earlier subsistence practices, transformed TÃ³rshavn from a modest administrative center into the economic hub of the Faroe Islands, concentrating population and trade activities there amid broader island-wide growth from approximately 8,000 residents in 1850 to 20,000 by 1920.[40]Parallel to economic changes, political aspirations for greater self-determination intensified, leading to a 1946 referendum where a slim majority favored independence from Denmark, though subsequent negotiations resulted in the Home Rule Act of March 23, 1948, effective April 1, which established the Faroe Islands as a self-governing community under the Danish Realm and transferred authority over internal affairsâincluding education, health, and local policingâto Faroese control while retaining Danish oversight of defense, foreign policy, and currency.[41][42] This framework fostered institutional growth in TÃ³rshavn, including the relocation and expansion of the LÃ¸gting (parliament) to the capital, symbolizing centralized governance.Post-World War II, the British occupation (1940â1945) introduced mechanized fishing vessels and industrial processing methods, accelerating TÃ³rshavn's role as a modern port and contributing to export-oriented growth, though ambitions for offshore oil extraction in the 1970s and subsequent decades yielded no commercially viable discoveries despite exploratory drilling confirming hydrocarbon presence.[43] Autonomy further expanded via the 2005 Foreign Policy Act, enabling the Faroese government to conduct independent negotiations on trade and fisheries agreements, such as those with the EU and Nordic states, while fisheries-dependent booms and bustsâexacerbated by international quota disputes akin to the Cod Warsâhighlighted vulnerabilities despite achieving a GDP per capita of approximately DKK 431,000 (around $65,000 USD nominal, higher in PPP terms) by 2021, driven primarily by aquaculture exports rather than Danish block grants, which constituted about 5% of GDP in recent years but proved critical during the 1990s banking crisis.[44][45][5][46]
Demographics
Population trends
As of January 2023, the TÃ³rshavn municipality recorded a population of approximately 23,000 residents, encompassing the urban core and adjacent suburbs such as HoyvÃk and Argir, which accounts for roughly 42% of the Faroe Islands' total population of 54,255.[47][48] This concentration reflects ongoing centralization, with the municipality experiencing one of the highest growth rates among Faroese regions, at 1.6% annually in recent periods driven by both natural increase and net migration.[49]Historically, TÃ³rshavn's population expanded slowly prior to 1900, remaining a modest administrative center with limited settlement due to the islands' dispersed fishing communities and harsh geography. Post-1950 growth accelerated markedly, fueled by infrastructure improvements, service consolidation, and economic pull factors like fishing industry modernization, raising the figure from under 10,000 in the mid-20th century to 19,330 by 2005.[50] This urbanization trend has positioned TÃ³rshavn as the demographic hub, with the municipality's share of the national population rising steadily amid broader Faroese recovery from earlier emigration waves.In recent years, growth has stabilized at around 1% annually, with projections estimating 22,470 residents by 2025, supported by a fertility rate of 2.05 children per woman offsetting modest domestic out-migration through inbound labor for sectors like tourism and aquaculture.[50][51] The urban density approaches 325 inhabitants per square kilometer across the municipality's 70.9 kmÂ², straining housing availability as construction lags behind demand, evidenced by rising property burdens reaching 44% of income in TÃ³rshavn and a surge in prices amid limited supply.[52] This pressure causally links to family formation patterns, where average household sizes hover near 2.1 children, amplifying needs for expanded residential capacity in a compact topographic setting.[51]
Ethnic and cultural composition
The population of TÃ³rshavn exhibits a high degree of ethnic homogeneity, with ethnic Faroese of primarily North Germanic (Norwegian and Icelandic) descent forming the overwhelming majority, estimated at around 95% based on national demographic patterns reflective of the capital's composition.[53] Genetic analyses confirm this uniformity, revealing a founder population shaped by Viking-era migrations from Scandinavia, with distinct paternal haplogroups (e.g., high frequencies of R1a subclades linked to Norse origins) and minimal subsequent admixture, underscoring isolation and endogamous practices that have preserved genetic continuity over centuries.[54][55]Immigration remains limited, accounting for roughly 5% of residents, predominantly Danes due to historical ties and small cohorts from Poland and other European nations, without significant dilution of the core ethnic profile.[53]Linguistically, Faroeseâa North Germanic tongue closely related to Icelandicâserves as the official language since its designation as the primary medium for administration, education, and public life under the 1948 Home Rule Act, with Danish retained as a secondary language for legal and inter-Nordic purposes.[56] This policy, coupled with cultural norms favoring linguistic endogamy and transmission through family and community traditions, has sustained Faroese's vitality amid external pressures, resisting assimilation into Danish despite centuries of colonial influence.[57]Religiously, the community is anchored in Lutheranism, with approximately 89% identifying as Christian, predominantly members of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of the Faroe Islands, reflecting lower rates of secularization than in mainland Scandinavia where affiliation has declined more sharply.[53] This enduring adherence, rooted in historical ties to Danish and Norwegian state churches, manifests in communal practices that integrate faith with identity preservation, without evidence of broader diversification in religious composition.[53]
Economy
Primary industries and resources
The economy of TÃ³rshavn, as the principal urban center and port of the Faroe Islands, centers on fishing and aquaculture, which constitute the primary industries and account for 90-95% of the archipelago's total export value.[45] These sectors generated exports valued at approximately DKK 11.9 billion in the 12 months ending August 2024, predominantly comprising salmon from aquaculture, cod, and pelagic species such as mackerel and herring processed through local facilities.[58] Demersal fish catches average around 130,000 tonnes annually, with the remainder from aquaculture emphasizing farmed Atlantic salmon, which has driven growth since the 1990s banking crisis by leveraging the islands' cold, clean waters for high-value production.[38]The TÃ³rshavn harbor serves as the critical asset for these activities, functioning as the largest port for containerized cargo and a base for the Faroese commercial fishing fleet, which includes long-liners, trawlers, purse seiners, and factory vessels targeting North Atlantic stocks.[59] This infrastructure supports operations that employ about 15% of the labor force and yield a trade surplus, with fish products exported mainly to the European Union, Denmark, the United Kingdom, and Russia.[45][60] Imports, conversely, consist primarily of fuels, machinery, and foodstuffs from Denmark (37% of total), Norway, and Germany, reflecting dependence on external energy sources given the absence of domestic production.[61]Secondary activities include small-scale ship repair and handicrafts, which contribute marginally to output but lack the scale to rival fisheries.[62] Unemployment remains low at around 1% as of mid-2025, sustained by fishing resilience and public sectoremployment rather than broad diversification.[63] Efforts to explore petroleum resources have confirmed an active hydrocarbon system through nine wells drilled to date, but no commercially viable reservoirs have been identified, underscoring the realism of prioritizing self-reliant marine sectors over unproven alternatives.[64] An annual block grant from Denmark, equivalent to about 2.4% of GDP in 2023 (DKK 616.8 million), bolsters fiscal stability but highlights structural vulnerabilities in transitioning to greater economic autonomy.[7]
Recent developments and challenges
Tourism in TÃ³rshavn and the Faroe Islands has rebounded post-COVID, with annual visitor numbers reaching approximately 110,000 by 2023, concentrated in summer months and supporting local businesses amid capacity strains from limited infrastructure.[65]Local food initiatives, such as the Matkovin project, have promoted Faroese producers through monthly farmers' markets in TÃ³rshavn, emphasizing fresh, regional ingredients to complement tourism growth.[66]Infrastructure upgrades include the July 2025 opening of Havnarvegur, featuring the 1,800-meter HÃºsareyn Tunnel, which connects HoyvÃk directly to the capital and alleviates traffic congestion in the urban core.[67] Recent additions like the ViÃ° Tjarnir multi-purpose arena, inaugurated in February 2025, host sports and cultural events, while expansions to four- and five-star hotels enhance capacity for conferences and visitors.[68][69]Fisheries challenges persist, with cod and haddock stocks described as severely overfished due to excess fleet capacity and poor stock conditions, contributing to unprofitability in demersal sectors.[70] Small-scale fishing operations face extinction risks from regulatory pressures and market shifts, as noted by family-run businesses in 2025.[71] A 2024 bilateral agreement with Greenland maintained stable reciprocal quotas for 2025, allowing Faroese vessels access to Greenlandic waters without reductions, though broader pelagic quota cuts loom for 2026 amid warnings of economic crisis from species like mackerel and herring.[72][73] The traditional pilot whale hunt (grindadrÃ¡p) draws sustainability debates, with critics citing health risks from contaminants like mercury in whale meat linked to neurological issues, while Faroese regulators maintain it as a regulated cultural practice with average annual catches of 600 whales.[74][75]Post-COVID economic recovery has been robust, with GDP growth in fixed prices reflecting strong performance in 2022 driven by fisheries and related exports, though the economy remains vulnerable to global fish price fluctuations that could exacerbate export risks.[76][77] Shipping and offshore activities have aided resilience, but dependence on aquaculture and wild catch exposes TÃ³rshavn's region to stock declines and disease outbreaks without diversification.[78]
Government and politics
Local administration and mayors
TÃ³rshavn Municipality, encompassing the capital and surrounding areas with an estimated population of 23,277 in 2025, is governed by an elected municipal council of 13 members and a mayor, with elections held every four years.[8][79] The council handles local services including infrastructure, welfare, and transport, exercising autonomy in areas such as taxation and fisheries management, while the Faroe Islands' broader self-governing framework under Danish sovereignty reserves defense, foreign affairs, and certain judicial appeals to Denmark.[80][2]The LÃ¸gting, the unicameral parliament of the Faroe Islands, convenes its sessions in TÃ³rshavn, with the annual opening traditionally held on ÃlavsÃ¸ka (July 29) at the LÃ¸gting House.[81] Local policies under municipal leadership include free public bus services within the municipality, implemented since 2007 for residents and extended to visitors in 2019, aimed at promoting efficient, low-emission mobility.[82][83]Mayoral leadership has shown continuity in administrative focus despite party shifts, with recent terms emphasizing pragmatic service delivery. Elsa Berg, aged 28, assumed office as mayor on January 1, 2025, succeeding HeÃ°in Mortensen and becoming the youngest in TÃ³rshavn's history; prior mayors include Mortensen (2021â2024), Poul Michelsen (1980â1991), and Lisbeth L. Petersen (1991â1997).[84][85]
Key political debates and autonomy issues
Debates over greater autonomy or full independence from Denmark have persisted in the Faroe Islands, with public opinion showing significant support for secession in recent polls. A September 2023 Spyr poll indicated 60% support for independence in a hypothetical referendum, reflecting growing sentiment for self-determination amid economic diversification away from Danish subsidies, which previously constituted a substantial portion of the budget but have diminished as fisheries and aquaculture exports boomed.[86] Pro-independence advocates, such as members of the TjÃ³Ã°veldi party, argue for economic self-reliance, citing the islands' control over resources like salmon farming and potential oil reserves as sufficient to sustain sovereignty without external aid.[87] Unionists, including the Sambandsflokkurin, counter that remaining in the Danish Realm ensures stability, defense, and access to markets, warning that independence could jeopardize welfare systems reliant on historical fiscal transfers.[88]Fisheries management underscores tensions between local sovereignty and international pressures, building on historical assertions of exclusive economic zones similar to Iceland's Cod Wars, though the Faroe Islands avoided direct naval confrontations. The islands maintain unilateral control over their EEZ, negotiating bilateral quotas that affirm self-determination, such as the 2025 agreements with the UK for mackerel and herring exchanges, and with Russia for cod despite geopolitical strains.[89][90] Critics of external interference, including EU quota disputes in prior mackerel wars, view such pressures as encroachments on Faroese rights to manage renewable resources vital to 90% of exports, prioritizing national interests over supranational regulations.[91]Domestic autonomy issues surfaced prominently in 2024 land reform protests, where farmers convoyed tractors into TÃ³rshavn to oppose a proposed bill seen as centralizing control over common grazing lands, threatening traditional sheep farming livelihoods central to rural self-sufficiency.[92] Opponents argued the reforms represented overreach by the LÃ¸gting into private and communal property rights, echoing broader concerns about balancing modernization with cultural preservation against state intervention. While the government framed the changes as necessary for sustainable land use, protesters highlighted risks to food security and local governance, illustrating fractures between urban policy in TÃ³rshavn and peripheral economic realities.[93] These events underscore ongoing debates on devolving authority to enhance local decision-making, with sovereignty proponents decrying dependencies that dilute Faroese causal control over territorial resources.
Culture and traditions
Traditional practices and controversies
The grindadrÃ¡p, a communal pilot whale drive hunt originating in the Viking era, remains a regulated tradition in the Faroe Islands, where pods are herded into designated bays for efficient slaughter using spinal lances to minimize time to insensibility. Annual catches average around 600 long-finned pilot whales, with the regional population estimated at 100,000 individuals, supported by scientific surveys indicating sustainability despite variable pod encounters.[94][75] This practice has historically contributed up to 30% of locally produced meat supply as of 2002, offering nutrient-dense blubber and meat vital for food security in the isolated archipelago, where imports were historically unreliable amid poverty and harsh conditions.[95]Animal rights groups, including Sea Shepherd and World Animal Protection, decry the grindadrÃ¡p as cruel, emphasizing graphic footage of family pods being driven ashore and slaughtered, with campaigns intensifying after the September 2021 hunt of 1,428 Atlantic white-sided dolphinsâthe largest on recordâand a 2023 "Don't Visit Faroe" boycott urging tourism avoidance.[96][97] Faroese regulators and proponents counter with evidence of low-impact harvestingâfar below reproductive ratesâand communal oversight ensuring hygiene and participation only when pods appear naturally, rejecting external ethical impositions that ignore causal necessities like protein access in pre-modern subsistence economies.[75] Consumption has declined due to mercury concerns in older whales, yet the hunt sustains social bonds and self-reliance without industrial alternatives.[98]Beyond hunting, the Faroese chain dance preserves medieval ring-dance origins, performed in interlocking circles with simple stepsâtwo forward, one backâwhile acapella singing of ballad poetry reinforces cultural memory and community cohesion during gatherings.[99] Traditional turf architecture, featuring thick grass-sod roofs over stone walls, exemplifies adaptive engineering for insulation and wind resistance, a Viking-derived method still visible in preserved structures that prioritize thermal efficiency over aesthetic modernism.[100] These practices underscore enduring causal realism in fostering resilience against environmental isolation, rather than yielding to decontextualized critiques.

Sir John Vincent Hurt (22 January 1940 – 25 January 2017) was an English actor. Regarded as one of the finest actors of his generation and described as having the "most distinctive voice in Britain",[1][2][3] he was referred to by David Lynch as "simply the greatest actor in the world".[4][5] In a career spanning more than five decades, he received numerous accolades, including four BAFTAs and a Golden Globe in addition to nominations for two Academy Awards. He was knighted in 2015 for his services to drama.
A graduate of Royal Academy of Dramatic Art, he came to prominence playing Richard Rich in the film A Man for All Seasons (1966) and won the British Academy Television Award for Best Actor for The Naked Civil Servant (1975). He played Caligula in the BBC TV series I, Claudius (1976). Hurt earned Academy Award nominations for Best Supporting Actor for Midnight Express (1978), and Best Actor for The Elephant Man (1980). Other films include Alien (1979), Heaven's Gate (1980), Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984), White Mischief (1987), Scandal (1989), The Field (1990), King Ralph (1991), Rob Roy (1995), and Contact (1997).[6]
Hurt gained further prominence portraying Garrick Ollivander in the Harry Potter film series (2001–11), as well as appearing in the 2004 and 2008 Hellboy films, V for Vendetta (2005), Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull (2008), Outlander (2008), and Snowpiercer (2013). He also acted in the acclaimed films Melancholia (2011), Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy (2011), Only Lovers Left Alive (2013) and Jackie (2016).
Hurt reprised his role as Quentin Crisp in An Englishman in New York (2009), which brought his seventh BAFTA nomination. He portrayed an incarnation of the Doctor known as the War Doctor in Doctor Who.[7][8] He voiced roles in Watership Down (1978), The Lord of the Rings (1978), The Plague Dogs (1982), The Black Cauldron (1985), Dogville (2003), Valiant (2005), Merlin (2008–2012), The Gruffalo's Child (2011), and Thomas & Friends: Sodor's Legend of the Lost Treasure (2015), and narrated the BBC documentary series Human Planet and Planet Dinosaur.
Life and career
[edit]Early years and education
[edit]John Vincent Hurt was born on 22 January 1940, in Chesterfield, Derbyshire,[9][10] the son of Arnould Herbert Hurt (1904–1999) and Phyllis (née Massey; 1907–1975). His father had been a mathematician, but became a Church of England clergyman and served as vicar of Holy Trinity Church in Shirebrook, Derbyshire; his mother, a one-time actress, became "the first female draughtsman" at Metropolitan-Vickers in Manchester.[11][12][13] In 1937, Hurt's father moved his family to Derbyshire, where he became Perpetual Curate of Holy Trinity Church. When Hurt was five, his father became the vicar of St Stephen's Church in Woodville, Derbyshire, and remained there until 1953.[14]
At the age of eight, Hurt was sent to the Anglican St Michael's Preparatory School in Otford, Kent,[15] where he eventually developed his passion for acting. He decided he wanted to become an actor after his first role as a girl in a school production of The Blue Bird by Maurice Maeterlinck.[16] Hurt stated that a senior master at the school would abuse him and others by removing his two false front teeth and putting his tongue in the boys' mouths, as well as rubbing their faces with his stubble, and that the experience affected him hugely.[17] Hurt, aged 12, became a boarder at Lincoln School (then a grammar school) because he had failed the entrance examination for admission to his brother's school. His headmaster at Lincoln School laughed when Hurt told him he wanted to be an actor, telling him, "Well, you may be alright in school plays but you wouldn't stand a chance in the profession."[18]
Hurt's father moved to St Aidan's Church in Cleethorpes, Lincolnshire. In a Guardian interview Hurt states the family lived in a vicarage opposite a cinema, but he was not allowed to go there, as films were "frowned upon." However, watching theatre was considered "fine" and encouraged particularly by his mother, who took him regularly to the repertory theatre in Cleethorpes. His parents disliked his later acting ambitions and encouraged him to become an art teacher instead.[18] Aged 17, Hurt enrolled in Grimsby Art School (now the East Coast School of Art and Design), where he studied art. In 1959, he won a scholarship allowing him to study for an Art Teacher's Diploma at Saint Martin's School of Art in London.[19] Despite the scholarship, paying his tuition fees and living expenses was difficult, so he persuaded some of his friends to pose naked and sold the portraits. In 1960, he won a scholarship to Royal Academy of Dramatic Art, where he trained for two years,[17] graduating in 1962 with an Acting (RADA Diploma).[20]
1962–1975
[edit]Hurt's first film role was as Phil Corbett in the Ralph Thomas directed British romantic drama The Wild and the Willing (1962). Hurt starred alongside Virginia Maskell and Paul Rogers.[21] In 1963 he acted in the Kitchen sink drama This Is My Street. The following year he appeared in the television series Gideon's Way episode: The Tin God (1964) as prison escapee Freddy Tisdale.
Hurt's first major role was as Richard Rich in the Fred Zinnemann directed historical drama film A Man for All Seasons (1966).[22] Hurt acted alongside Paul Scofield, Wendy Hiller, Orson Welles, Robert Shaw, Susannah York, and Vanessa Redgrave. The film received critical acclaim and six Academy Awards including Best Picture. Hurt then acted in the British romantic drama The Sailor from Gibraltar starring Jeanne Moreau directed by Tony Richardson. He then starred in John Huston's raunchy adventure comedy Sinful Davey (1969) which critics compared to the film Tom Jones. That same year he acted in the British war film Before Winter Comes opposite David Niven and the drama In Search of Gregory alongside Julie Christie.
He then played Timothy Evans, who was hanged for murders committed by his landlord John Christie, in 10 Rillington Place (1971), earning him his first BAFTA nomination for Best Supporting Actor. His portrayal of Quentin Crisp in the TV play The Naked Civil Servant (1975) gave him prominence and earned him the British Academy Television Award for Best Actor.[22] The following year, Hurt appeared as Anthony John Grey, a crooked computer programming expert in The Sweeney episode Tomorrow Man.
1976–1980
[edit]He won further acclaim for his bravura performance as the Roman emperor Caligula in the BBC drama serial I, Claudius (1976). In a much later documentary about the series, I Claudius: A Television Epic (2002), Hurt revealed that he had originally declined the role when it was first offered to him, but that series director Herbert Wise had invited him to a special pre-production party, hoping Hurt would change his mind, and that he was so impressed by meeting the rest of the cast and crew that he reversed his decision and took the role.[23]
Hurt appeared in the 1978 film Midnight Express, for which he won a Golden Globe and a BAFTA and was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor (the latter of which he lost to Christopher Walken for his performance in The Deer Hunter).[23] Around the same time, he lent his voice to Ralph Bakshi's animated film adaptation of The Lord of the Rings, playing the role of Aragorn. Hurt voiced Hazel, the heroic rabbit leader of his warren in the film adaptation of Watership Down (both 1978) and later played the major villain, General Woundwort, in the animated television series version.[24]
His other roles in the 1970s and the beginning of the 1980s included Kane, the first victim of the title creature in the Ridley Scott directed film Alien (1979). He reprised the role as a parody in Spaceballs. In 1980 he portrayed the deformed Joseph Merrick in David Lynch's biographical drama film The Elephant Man (1980). Hurt starred alongside Anthony Hopkins, John Gielgud, and Anne Bancroft. Peter Bradshaw of The Guardian praised his performance writing, "John Hurt, in complex and intricate prosthetics, plays Merrick with an unforgettably distinctive, gentle, quavering voice".[25] He won another the BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role. He was also nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actor and the Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Motion Picture Drama.[22]
That same year he starred in Michael Cimino's epic Western Heaven's Gate starring Kris Kristofferson, Christopher Walken, and Sam Waterston. The following year he portrayed Jesus Christ in the Mel Brooks comedy film History of the World, Part I (1981). Also in 1981 he starred in Delbert Mann's thriller Night Crossing (1981). He earned the Evening Standard British Film Award for Best Actor for his performances as Bob Champion in the sports drama Champions (1984), Mitchell Braddock in the crime thriller The Hit (1984), and Winston Smith in Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984). He also played the would-be art school radical Scrawdyke in Little Malcolm (1974).
1981–1999
[edit]Hurt also had a starring role in Sam Peckinpah's critically panned but moderately successful final film, The Osterman Weekend (1983). Also in this period, he starred as the Fool opposite Laurence Olivier's King in King Lear (1983). Hurt also appeared as Raskolnikov in a BBC television adaptation of Crime and Punishment (1979).[26]
Hurt voiced Snitter in The Plague Dogs, played Winston Smith in the film adaptation of George Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984) and starred in Disney's The Black Cauldron (1985), voicing the film's main antagonist, the Horned King. Hurt provided the voiceover for AIDS: Iceberg/Tombstone,[27] a 1986 public information film warning of the dangers of AIDS, and played the title role, the on-screen narrator, in Jim Henson's television series The StoryTeller (1988). Hurt appeared in the 1987 Bob Clark-directed movie From the Hip.
He had a supporting role as "Bird" O'Donnell in Jim Sheridan's film The Field (1990), which garnered him another BAFTA nomination. In this film, Hurt starred alongside Richard Harris who earned a nomination for the Academy Award for Best Actor. In King Ralph (1991) Hurt played Lord Percival Graves. Hurt portrayed James Graham, 1st Duke of Montrose in the historical drama Rob Roy opposite Liam Neeson, Jessica Lange and Tim Roth. That same year he acted in the Jim Jarmusch directed Western Dead Man starring Johnny Depp, and Walter Hill's Western Wild Bill (1995) with Jeff Bridges.
In 1997 he starred in Richard Kwietniowski's Love and Death on Long Island for which he was nominated for the BIFA for Best Performance by an Actor in a British Independent Film. He was cast as the reclusive tycoon S. R. Hadden in Contact (1997).[24] During this time, Hurt provided narration on the British musical group Art of Noise's concept album The Seduction of Claude Debussy and narrated a four-part TV series The Universe (1999).[28]
2000–2017
[edit]In the first Harry Potter film, Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (2001), he played Mr Ollivander, the wand-maker. He returned for the adaptation of Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, though his scenes in that film were cut. He also returned for Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows Part 1 and Part 2. In the 2006 film V for Vendetta, he played the role of Adam Sutler, leader of the Norsefire fascist dictatorship and in Steven Spielberg's Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull (2008) he appeared as Harold Oxley.[29]
He voiced the Great Dragon Kilgharrah, who aids the young warlock Merlin as he protects the future King Arthur, in the BBC television series Merlin (also 2008).[30] In 2011, he narrated the BBC documentary Planet Dinosaur, a dinosaur-centered documentary completely shown through CGI.[31]
More than thirty years after The Naked Civil Servant, Hurt reprised the role of Quentin Crisp in the 2009 film An Englishman in New York. This television film depicts Crisp's later years in New York.[32] He returned to Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, playing the on-screen Big Brother for the Paper Zoo Theatre Company's stage adaptation of the novel in June 2009. The theatre production premiered at the National Media Museum, in Bradford and toured in 2010. Hurt said, "I think Paper Zoo thought it would be quite ironic to have the person who played Winston having risen in the party. From the Chestnut Tree Cafe, he's managed to get his wits together again, now understanding that 2 and 2 make 5, and becomes Big Brother. So it tickled my fancy, and of course, I looked up Paper Zoo, and they seem to me to be the sort of company that's essential in the country as we know it, and doing a lot of really good stuff."[33]
At the 65th British Academy Film Awards Hurt won the award for Outstanding British Contribution to Cinema. In 2013, Hurt first appeared in the Doctor Who episode "The Name of the Doctor" as an unplaced incarnation of the Doctor.[34] His character is named as the War Doctor in the mini-episode "The Night of the Doctor"; his character is given focus in the 50th anniversary episode "The Day of the Doctor",[34] He reprised the role on audio for Big Finish Productions in a series of audio stories starting from 2015 to 2017, completing twelve episodes over four box sets.[35] He also played the title character in an audio drama adaptation of The Invisible Man for the company, for which he was nominated for a BBC Audio Drama Award.[36][37]
During Terry Gilliam's eighth attempt at making his development hell project The Man Who Killed Don Quixote, Hurt was set to star as Don Quixote alongside Adam Driver. However, his declining health and eventual death led the project to be cancelled yet again; he was eventually replaced by Jonathan Pryce.[38][39]
Hurt was due to appear alongside Ben Kingsley in a film entitled Broken Dream, to be directed by Neil Jordan.[40] In 2015, Hurt guest stars as the voice of Sailor John, the main antagonist in the Thomas & Friends film Sodor's Legend of the Lost Treasure along with Eddie Redmayne (Ryan) and Jamie Campbell Bower (Skiff).[41] At the time of his death he had completed filming That Good Night, in which he played a terminally ill writer.[42] Hurt was initially cast as Neville Chamberlain in Darkest Hour. However, according to Gary Oldman, Hurt was undergoing treatment for pancreatic cancer, and dropped the role in pre-production; actor Ronald Pickup assumed the role of Chamberlain instead.[43]
Personal life
[edit]Hurt had an older brother, Brother Anselm (born Michael Hurt in 1932[44][45]), a Roman Catholic convert who became a monk and writer at Glenstal Abbey after moving there in 1996;[46] Hurt contributed to his brother's books.[47][new archival link needed] In early 2012, Anselm, now retired, was arrested over child abuse allegations that took place in the late 1960s while he was working at a boarding school in Bath, Somerset.[46][48][49][50] Anselm died in 2023.[44]
Hurt also had an adopted sister, Monica. She is mentioned in accounts of John Hurt's upbringing and his brother's move to Catholicism. Monica passed away from variant CJD in 2005. [51]
In 1962, Hurt's father left his parish in Cleethorpes to become headmaster of St Michael's College in the Central American country of British Honduras. Hurt's mother died in 1975, and his father died in 1999 at the age of 95.
In 1962, Hurt married actress Annette Robertson. The marriage ended in 1964. In 1967, he began his longest relationship with Marie-Lise Volpeliere-Pierrot, a French model. The couple had planned to get married after 15 years together. On 26 January 1983, Hurt and Volpeliere-Pierrot went horse riding early in the morning near their house in Ascott-under-Wychwood, Oxfordshire; Volpeliere-Pierrot was thrown from her horse. She fell into a coma and died later that day.[52]
In September 1984, Hurt married his old friend, Donna Peacock, an American actress, at a local Register Office. The couple moved to Kenya but divorced in January 1990.[citation needed]
On 24 January 1990, Hurt married Joan Dalton, an American production assistant,[24] whom he had met while filming Scandal. With her, he had two sons. This marriage ended in 1996 and was followed by a seven-year relationship with Sarah Owens, a Dublin-born presenter and writer. The couple moved to County Wicklow, where they settled close to their friends, director John Boorman and Claddagh Records founder and Guinness heir Garech Browne. In July 2002, the couple separated. In March 2005, Hurt married his fourth wife, Anwen Rees-Meyers, an advertising film producer. He gave up smoking and drinking during his fourth marriage.[53] He lived in Cromer, Norfolk.[54]
In 2007, Hurt took part in the BBC genealogical television series Who Do You Think You Are?, which investigated part of his family history. Prior to the programme, Hurt had harboured a love of Ireland and was enamoured of a "deeply beguiling" family legend that suggested his great-grandmother had been the illegitimate daughter of a Marquess of Sligo. The genealogical evidence uncovered seemed to contradict the family legend, rendering the suggestion doubtful. The search revealed that his great-grandmother had previously lived in Grimsby, at a location within a mile of the art college at which Hurt had been a student.[55]
In 2016, Hurt announced he was in favour of the United Kingdom voting to remain in the EU.[56]
Illness and death
[edit]On 16 June 2015, Hurt publicly announced that he had been diagnosed with early-stage pancreatic cancer.[57] He confirmed that he would continue to work while undergoing treatment and said that both he and the medical team treating him were "more than optimistic about a satisfactory outcome".[58] Following treatment, he stated that his cancer was in remission on 12 October 2015.[59] Hurt died at his home in Cromer, Norfolk, on 25 January 2017.[60][61]

Honours and distinctions
[edit]In the 2004 Birthday Honours, Hurt was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) "for services to drama".[62]
Hurt was awarded a Fellow of the British Film Institute in 2009.[63] In 2012, he was among the British cultural icons selected by artist Sir Peter Blake to appear in a new version of his album cover for the Beatles' Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, to celebrate the British cultural figures of his life that he most admired.[64][65] In 2014, he received the Will Award, presented by the Shakespeare Theatre Company, along with Stacy Keach and Dame Diana Rigg. The John Hurt Centre opened in September 2016 and is an education and exhibition space located at Cinema City, Norwich.[66]
He was knighted in the 2015 New Year Honours also "for services to drama".[67][68] On 17 July 2015, he attended an investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle where he received the accolade from Queen Elizabeth II.[69]
Honorary academic degrees and appointments
[edit]Hurt received an Honorary Doctor of Literature (Hon.D.Litt.) degree from the University of Derby in 2002.[70] In 2006, he received an Honorary Doctor of Letters (Hon.D.Litt.) degree from the University of Hull.[71] In 2012, he was appointed provost of Norwich University College of the Arts,[72] and became its first chancellor when the college became a full university in 2013.[73][74] In 2013, he was given an Honorary Doctor of Arts (Hon.D.A) degree by the University of Lincoln, at Lincoln Cathedral.[75]
Charity patronage
[edit]Since 2003, Hurt was a patron of the Proteus Syndrome Foundation, both in the United Kingdom and in the US.[76] Proteus syndrome is the condition that Joseph Merrick, who Hurt played (renamed as John Merrick) in The Elephant Man, is thought to have suffered from, although Merrick's exact condition is still not known with certainty.[77][78][79][80]
From 2006, Hurt had been a patron of Project Harar, a UK-based charity working in Ethiopia for children with facial disfigurements.[81] Hurt was announced as patron of Norwich Cinema City in March 2013.[82]
In 2014, Hurt designed a Paddington Bear statue which was placed outside the British Museum. It was one of fifty statues of Paddington located around London prior to the release of the film Paddington which were auctioned to raise funds for the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC).[83]

The BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role is an award presented annually by the British Academy of Film and Television Arts (BAFTA). It has been awarded since the 6th British Academy Film Awards to an actor who has delivered an outstanding performance in a leading role in a film. From 1952 to 1967, there were two Best Actor awards: one for a British actor and another for a foreign actor. In 1968, the two prizes of British and Foreign actor were combined to create a single Best Actor award. Its current title, for Best Actor in a Leading Role, has been used since 1995.
Peter Finch has the most wins in the category with five. The most recent winner of the award is Robert Aramayo for I Swear (2025).

Cilicia (/sɪˈlɪʃə/, sil-ISH-ə)[3][note 1] is a geographical region of southern Anatolia in West Asia, extending inland from the northeastern coasts of the Mediterranean Sea. Cilicia borders Pamphylia to the west, Lycaonia and Cappadocia to the north, Commagene to the north-east, Syria to the east and the Mediterranean Sea to the south. Cilicia has a population ranging over six million, concentrated mostly at the Cilician plain (Turkish: Çukurova). The region includes the provinces of Mersin, Adana, Osmaniye and Hatay.
Name
[edit]The name of Cilicia (Κιλικία) was derived from the Akkadian toponym Ḫilakku (𒆳𒄭𒋃𒆪[5]), which was the name used by the Neo-Assyrian Empire to designate the western part of what would become Cilicia.[6][7]
The English spelling Cilicia is the same as the Latin, as it was transliterated directly from the Greek form Κιλικία. The palatalization of c occurring in Western Europe in later Vulgar Latin (c. 500–700) accounts for its modern pronunciation in English.
Geography
[edit]Cilicia is located on the southern coast of Anatolia, and it historically extended from Coracesium or the river Melas in the west to the Amanus Mountains in the east, while to the north and northwest it was bounded by the Taurus Mountains, which are passable in very few places, such as the Cilician Gates, and in the south it was bounded by the Gulf of Iskenderun.[6][8]
Cilicia consisted of two main contrasting regions:[7][9]
- to the west was a mountainous region characterised by rough terrain, corresponding to the Neo-Assyrian period territory of Ḫilakku and the Graeco-Roman region of Rough Cilicia;
- to the east was a flat and water-rich fertile region defined by a smooth terrain, corresponding to the Neo-Assyrian period territory of Ḫiyawa and the Graeco-Roman region of Plain Cilicia.
The western mountainous part of Cilicia was called Rugged Cilicia or Rough Cilicia (Ancient Greek: Κιλικία Τραχεῖα, romanized: Kilikía Trakheîa; Latin: Cilicia Aspera), while the eastern region was dominated by the alluvial plain of the rivers Cydnus, Sarus, and Pyramus, and was therefore known as Plain Cilicia or Flat Cilicia (Ancient Greek: Κιλικία Πεδιάς, romanized: Kilikía Pediás; Latin: Cilicia Campestris).[6]
Although Cilicia's boundaries are difficult to traverse, it has important access routes which have connected it since antiquity with the neighbouring North Syrian Plain in the east and the Anatolian Highlands in the north:[10]
- the most important of these passages across the Taurus Mountains are the course of the Göksu River which ends near Mut to the southeast of Konya, and the Cilician Gates to the north of Tarsus which opens on Porsuk near Tyana. The upper reaches of the Seyhan and Ceyhan rivers were however more difficult to cross and were therefore of little importance for trade in antiquity.
- two important passes also allowed passage through the Amanus Mountains: the Amanian Gate, now known as the Bahçe Pass, led into the plain of İslahiye, which was a side valley of the Amuq Plain in Hatay; as well as the southern Amanus Pass or Syrian Gates, now known as the Beilan Pass, which laid at the end of a southern route branching off at Osmaniye and following the coast through Issus and İskenderun, and opened into the Orontes Plain near Alalaḫ or Antioch. These two routes provided access from Cilicia to the plains of the northern Levant and Mesopotamia.
The most important route of the Cilician Plain, since antiquity, has run from the Amanus passes to the Taurus passes. This route comes from northern Syria, crosses Plain Cilica westward through Adana and Tarsus, and finally continues into Anatolia. In modern times, this route corresponds to the trajectory of a motorway, a national highway, and the Baghdad Railway built in the early 20th century AD. The distribution of ancient settlements along this axis suggests that this route existed from as early as the Chalcolithic Period.[10]
Salamis, the city on the east coast of Cyprus, was included in the Roman province of Cilicia from 58 BC until 27 BC.
Rough Cilicia
[edit]Rough Cilicia (Ancient Greek: Κιλικία Τραχεῖα, romanized: Kilikía Trakheîa; Latin: Cilicia Aspera; Neo-Assyrian Akkadian: 𒆳𒄭𒋃𒆪, romanized: Ḫilakku;[5] Neo-Babylonian Akkadian: 𒆳𒉿𒆸𒁺, romanized: Pirindu[11])[12][13][14] is a rugged mountain district[15] formed by the spurs of Taurus, which often terminate in rocky headlands with small sheltered harbours,[16] features which, in classical times, made the coast a string of havens for pirates[16][17] and, in the Middle Ages, outposts for Genoese and Venetian traders. The district is watered by the Calycadnus[18] and was covered in ancient times by forests that supplied timber to Phoenicia and Egypt. Cilicia lacked large cities.[19]
Plain Cilicia
[edit]Plain Cilicia (Ancient Greek: Κιλικία Πεδιάς, romanized: Kilikía Pediás; Latin: Cilicia Campestris; Neo-Assyrian Akkadian: 𒆳𒄣𒂊, romanized: Que;[20] Neo-Babylonian Akkadian: 𒆳𒄷𒈨𒂊, romanized: Ḫuwê[21][22]), to the east, included the rugged spurs of Taurus and a large coastal plain, with rich loamy soil,[19] known to Greeks such as Xenophon (who passed through with his mercenary group of the Ten Thousand,[23]) for its abundance (euthemia),[24] filled with sesame and millet and olives[25] and pasturage for the horses imported into ancient Israel by King Solomon.[26] Many of its high places were fortified.
The plain is watered by multiple rivers originating in the Tauris Mountains, with the three most important of these being:[8]
- the Berdan River (Ancient Greek: Κύδνος, romanized: Kúdnos; Latin: Cydnus),
- the Seyhan River (Ancient Greek: Σάρος, romanized: Sáros; Latin: Sarus),
- and the Ceyhan River (Ancient Greek: Πύραμος, romanized: Púramos; Latin: Pyramus).
Climate
[edit]The climate of Cilicia shows significant differences between the mountains and the lower plains. At the lower plains, the climate reflects a typical Mediterranean style; summers are hot[27] while winters are mild, making the land, particularly, the eastern plains, fertile.[28] In the coldest month (January), the average temperature is 9 °C, and in the warmest month (August), the average temperature is 28 °C. The mountains of Cilicia have an inland climate with snowy winters. The average annual precipitation in the region is 647 mm and the average number of rainy days in a year is 76. Mersin and surrounding areas have the highest average temperature in Cilicia. Mersin also has high annual precipitation (1096 mm) and 85 rainy days in a year.
The Cilician Plain possesses fertile soils, a hot climate, and abundant water resources thanks to enough rainfalls and multiple rivers, which make it one of the most productive agricultural regions of present-day Turkey. A large number of burial mounts from every era of human presence there shows that these favourable conditions have been conducive to intensive human settlement in Plain Cilicia from the Neolithic Period.[29]
Geology
[edit]This section needs additional citations for verification. (April 2026) |
The mountains of Cilicia are formed from ancient limestones, conglomerate, marlstone, and similar materials. The Taurus Mountains are composed of karstic limestone, while its soil is also limestone-derived, with pockets of volcanic soil.[30] The lower plain is an extremely important alluvial plain in Turkey.[31] Expansion of limestone formations and fourth-era alluvials brought by the rivers Seyhan and Ceyhan formed the plains of the region over the course of time.
Akyatan, Akyayan, Salt Lake, Seven lakes at Aladağ, and Karstik Dipsiz lake near Karaisalı are the lakes of the region. The reservoirs in the region are Seyhan, Çatalan, Yedigöze, Kozan and Mehmetli.
The major rivers in Cilicia are Seyhan, Ceyhan, Berdan (Tarsus), Asi and Göksu.
- Seyhan River emerges from the confluence of Zamantı and Göksu rivers which originate from Kayseri Province and flows into the Gulf of Mersin. The river is 560 km long.
- Ceyhan River emerges from the confluence of the Aksu and Hurman rivers and flows towards Cape Hürmüz at the Gulf of İskenderun. It is 509 km long and it forms the Akyayan, Akyatan, and Kakarat lakes before flowing into the Mediterranean.
- Berdan River originates from the Taurus Mountains and flows into the Mediterranean south of Tarsus.
- Göksu river originates from the Taurus Mountains and flows into the Mediterranean 16 km southeast of Silifke. It forms the Göksu Delta, including Akgöl Lake and Paradeniz Lagoon.
History
[edit]Plain Cilicia formed an important link between Syria, and, by extension, Mesopotamia and Egypt as well, with Cyprus and the Anatolian highlands for several periods.[29]
Neolithic
[edit]Due to its propitious environmental conditions, Plain Cilicia has been intensively settled by humans since the Neolithic Period.[29]
During the Neolithic Period, ceramic wares from Cilicia show links to northern Syria and northern Mesopotamia, as well as to the ceramics of Inner Anatolia. Influences from the Halaf culture of northern Mesopotamia are visible in Cilicia in this period, and so are influences from the Ubaid culture.[29]
Chalcolithic
[edit]During the Chalcolithic Period, close contacts existed between Cilicia and the Amuq E and F cultures of the nearby Amuq Plain.[33]
During the Late Chalcolithic Period, when the Uruk culture spread in Mesopotamia, Cilicia exhibited closer cultural links to the Anatolian Highlands.[33]
Bronze Age
[edit]Beginning in the Early Bronze Age II period, and especially during the Early Bronze Age III period, which corresponds to the Early Bronze Age I-IV of the northern Levant, Syrian-Levantine influence on Cilician pottery was more intensely felt, resulting in the appearance of special types of pottery such as Metallic Ware and Syrian Flasks.[33] Thus, Cilicia moved away from influence by the Anatolian cultural sphere and towards the northern Syrian cultural zone during the early Bronze Age, with this latter one persisting until the Middle Bronze Age.[34]
Cilicia is not mentioned in any ancient texts in the 3rd millennium BC, and even the sources of Ebla do not refer to it.[33]
The first recognisable mentions of the Cilician Plain instead are from between c. 2000 and c. 1750 BC, with the Story of Sinuhe, which takes place during the reign of Senusret I (r. 1971 – 1926 BC), referring to a ḫantawattis from the south of the land of Kawa, who can be located in Plain Cilicia; the Luwian title of this ruler shows that the ruling class of Cilicia during this period were Luwians.[33]
An Egyptian inscription from the reign of Senusret I's successor, Amenemhat II (r. 1929 – 1895 BC), mentioned the port city of Ura. There is otherwise no information about the political situation of Cilicia from the period lasting from c. 2000 to c. 1500 BC, with neither the letters of Assyrian traders in Kaniš nor the royal correspondence of the palace at Mari providing any information about Cilicia.[35]
Archaeological remains from this period derive almost solely from Tarsus, Mersin, Kinet Höyük and Sirkeli Höyük. Beginning in the Bronze Age IA, which is when the land of Kawa was mentioned in the Story of Sinuhe, Painted Syro-Cilician Ware became prevalent in large parts of the Levant and Syria, which, in addition to its similarities with Khabur Ware and Levantine Painted Ware, showed close connections between Cilicia and these regions. Contacts between Cilicia and Central Anatolia are discernible in the forms of the ceramics, such as spouted jugs found at Sirkeli Höyük, as well as by the dominance of Central Anatolian house types at Tarsus and Mersin.[35]
Before the end of the Middle Bronze Age, the Hurrian language and religion had spread into Cilicia, where the Hurrian and Luwian components were dominant among the population of the region from the period lasting from c. 1500 to c. 1250 BC.[36]
During the Late Bronze Age, Cilicia was dominated by the kingdom of Kizzuwatna which came into existence during the middle of the 2nd millennium BC, at the time of the Hittite king Ammuna, and was an independent power as well as a buffer between the Hittite Empire and the kingdom of Mitanni.[36] During this period, silver from this region was exported to Middle Kingdom Egypt.[6]
Even at this early period, Kizzuwatna was an important location for the Hittite Empire, since it provided the Hittites with access to Syria, which was useful for trade and was strategically advantageous.[37]
The border between Kizzuwatna and the Hittite kingdom was established by the treaty between Šunaššura of Kizzuwatna and Tudḫaliya I/II of the Hittites, according to which Kizzuwatna's most western city was to be Pitura on the coast and opposite of Lamiya (Classical Lamos), thus leaving the port-city of Ura under Hittite rule. Meanwhile, the southwest–northeast border of Kizzuwatna ran through the Taurus Mountains and included the upper reaches of the Šamri (Classical Saros) river.[37]
Kizzuwatna was later annexed by the Hittites, possibly during the reigns of Arnuwanda I or Šuppiluliuma I, the latter of whom appointed Kantuzzili, and later Telipinu, as priest at Kummanni.[36] The incorporation of Kizzuwatna into the Hittite Empire allowed Šuppiluliuma I to engage in an aggressively expansionist policy in Syria.[37]
Kizzuwatna had a significant cultural influence on the Hittite Empire: its Hurrian and Luwian populations and being open to Syria, it influenced Hittite religion in many aspects.[37]
In the Middle Bronze Age developed a far-reaching economic and socio-political system across the eastern Mediterranean, which was maintained by the palaces, and would reach its peak in the Late Bronze Age. Because of the dominance of the secular ruling classes in the economic, poilitical and ideological domains, it is referred to in research as a "Bronze Age palace culture," characterised by a reciprocal exchange system which included trade and prestige goods, craftsmen, and ideas. Evidence of this system is visible in the archaeological finds and texts from palaces like Knossos in Crete, Avaris in Egypt, Hattusa in Anatolia, and Ugarit, Alalaḫ and Qatna in the Levant, although the processes through which this interregional cultural exchange unfolded are still poorly understood.[38]
The extent to which Cilicia was integrated into this international system, in which form did a palace culture develop there, and the degree to which it participated in the widespread exchange of luxury goods are also still currently unknown; until the present day, no palaces have been found and excavated in Cilicia. It is therefore also impossible to know which architectural styles from surrounding areas were borrowed by Cilician architecture, and whether certain luxury goods were imported and imitated there, as was the case in Syria.[38]
The second half of the Late Bronze Age in Cilicia is characterised by Hittite Drab Ware and Red Lustrous Wheelmade Ware, whose origin was either from Cilicia itself or from Cyprus. Several Cypriot pottery imports and isolated Mycenaean shards also appeared in Tarsus at the same time as this ware, thus providing an outline of the cultural exchanges under way at this time. Influence from Central Anatolia was especially intense, as attested by the city wall in Mersin, which used the box-and-beam masonry technique based on Hittite models.[39]
Iron Age
[edit]With the Bronze Age Collapse, Kizzuwatna also came to an end, and from its remains several local states emerged in Cilicia, which therefore became dominated by two main polities:[6][40][41]
- in the east was Ḫiyawa, corresponding to Plain Cilicia, and referred to as Que in Neo-Assyrian sources and as Ḫuwê in Neo-Babylonian sources;[42]
- in the west, corresponding to Rough Cilicia, was the state referred to as Ḫilakku in Neo-Assyrian sources and as Pirindu in Neo-Babylonian sources.[43]
Both Hiyawa and Hilakku came under pressure from the Neo-Assyrian Empire from the 9th century BC, and more so in the 8th century BC, when they were temporarily annexed and made into Neo-Assyrian provinces.[41] During the 1st millennium BC, silver from Cilicia was exported to Assyria.[6]
During the 8th to 7th centuries BC, Greek traders and colonists established settlements on the Cilician coasts, such as Nagidos and Celenderis founded by Samos, Soli founded by Lindos; Greeks also established themselves in local settlements, such as at Anchiale and Tarsus.[44][6]

Following the collapse of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, an independent state, called Cilicia (Ancient Greek: Κιλικία, romanized: Kilikía) by the ancient Greeks, was established in southeastern Anatolia in the 6th century BC under the rule of a native dynasty,[45] with its capital at the city of Tarsus.[46][6][7]
Submission to the Achaemenid Empire
[edit]In the mid-6th century BC, the kingdom of Cilicia supported the founding king of the Persian Achaemenid Empire, Cyrus II, in his wars against Croesus of Lydia,[47] as a consequence of which Cilicia became a vassal of the Achaemenid empire as from c. 542 BC,[7] and the Cilician rulers became part of the Achaemenid administration.[47]
Under early Achaemenid rule, Cilicia maintained a significant degree of autonomy[7] and the native rulers at Tarsus acted as satraps (governors) for the Achaemenid administration, with their authority extending until as far west as Aspendus.[47][6]
Cilicia remained under efficient administration, and it would continue to provide troops for the Achaemenid wars in Anatolia, Egypt and Cyprus.[47]

Satrapy of Cilicia
[edit]In 401 BC, the Achaemenid king of kings Artaxerxes II abolished the autonomy of Cilicia in reaction to the local Cilician ruler Syennesis III's support for the rebellion of Cyrus the Younger,[47] resulting in the kingdom of Cilicia being abolished and fully integrated into the Achaemenid empire as a normal province ruled by and appointed by the Achaemenid king of kings, which it would remain until the end of the Achaemenid Empire in 333 BC.[47][7][48]
Once the revolt of Cyrus the Younger had been suppressed, Cilicia was again used as an assembly point for Achaemenid forces in preparation for military action in the Aegean Sea during 396 to 395 BC, and against Cyprus in the 380s BC.[47]
During the 390s BC, Camisares was appointed as satrap of Cilicia. Camisares was himself succeeded by his son, Datames, who eventually became the satrap of both Cilicia and Cappadocia until his assassination in c. 362 BC.[47]
In the 340s BC, the satrap of Cilicia was Mazaeus, who was also given authority over Syria as reward for his service in a campaign against Egypt.[47]
Hellenistic period
[edit]Following the Battle of Issus, Cilicia became part of the empire of Alexander III of Macedon[6] after he entered the region through the Cilician Gates in the Taurus Mountains without facing any resistance.[46]
Alexander forded the Halys River in the summer of 333 BC, ending up on the border of southeastern Phrygia and Cilicia. He knew well the writings of Xenophon, and how the Cilician Gates had been "impassable if obstructed by the enemy". Alexander reasoned that by force alone he could frighten the defenders and break through, and he gathered his men to do so. In the cover of night, they attacked, startling the guards and sending them and their satrap into full flight, setting their crops aflame as they made for Tarsus. This good fortune allowed Alexander and his army to pass unharmed through the Gates and into Cilicia.[49]
During Alexander III's invasion, a lesser officer named Arsames who had fled to Cilicia from the northwest to organise new resistance there defended it against the Macedonian forces.[47]
During the Hellenistic period, Cilicia became disputed between the Ptolemaic Kingdom and the Seleucid Empire, with the latter being mostly in control of it, while the Teucrid dynasty ruled at the city of Olba.[46]
Although no later Persian empire ever regained control of Cilicia, one Seleucid officer named Aribazus and attested as administrator of Cilicia in 246 BC was possibly of Persian descent.[47]
During the Hellenistic era, numerous cities were established in Cilicia, which minted coins showing the badges (gods, animals, and objects) associated with each polis.[50]
The Seleucids, especially Antiochus IV, focused on Hellenising Cilicia by establishing or rebuilding several poleis, such as Seleucia on the Calycadnus, Antioch on the Cydnus (Tarsus), Seleucia on the Pyramus (Mopsuestia), Hierapolis (Castabala), and Epiphaneia.[51]
In the 3rd century BC, sporadic Ptolemaic presence was attested in Rugged Cilicia.[52]
With the weakening of the Seleucid kingdom in the late 2nd century BC, piracy spread in the Mediterranean which had its main bases in Rugged Cilicia.[46][52]
Roman and Byzantine periods
[edit]In 102 BC, the Roman Republic established a provincia of the praetor Marcus Antonius in Cilicia to fight the Cilician pirates, with the command being renewed repeatedly.[46][52][53]
In 83 BC, the Armenian king Tigranes II conquered Plain Cilicia, and he deported Cilicians to Tigranocerta.[52]
Between 78 and 74 BC, Publius Servilius Vatia Isauricus conquered the population of Rugged Cilicia, which made a permanent Roman presence in Cilicia possible.[52][53]
In 69 BC, Lucullus returned the Cilician deportees to Tigranocerta back to their homeland.[52]
After Pompey was given the imperium proconsulare maius, he was able to defeat the Cilician pirates in 67 BC, and he arranged for his defeated enemies to be settled in Pompeiopolis (formerly Soli) and other depopulated Cilician towns. This victory strengthened the Roman presence in Cilicia,[52][53] and in 64 BC the province was extended to include Plain Cilicia.[46]
In 56 BC, the province of Cilicia was temporarily extended to include a large inland territory reaching Phrygia so that it could protect the province of Asia and made the presence of a Roman garrison there unnecessary.[46]
In 51 BC, the Parthian Empire was able to take advantage of the weakness of the Roman Republic to invade Cilicia (Parthian: 𐭊𐭉𐭋𐭊𐭉𐭀).[47]
In 51 or 50 BC, the proconsul Cicero successfully campaigned in Cilicia against the Eleutherokilikes in the Amanus Mountains, which further solidified the Roman presence in CIlicia.[52][53]
After Julius Caesar's death, the provincia of Cilicia was dissolved in 43 BC, and most of Rugged Cilicia was given to Amyntas of Galatia, then to Archelaus of Cappadocia. Plain Cilicia meanwhile was ruled by the kingdom of Tarcondimotus I as well as other smaller client-states of the Roman Republic, or administered as part of Syria.[46][52][53]
Tarcondimotus I had supported the losing side of both Roman civil wars by offering naval support to Pompey and Mark Antony, due to which his son Tarcondimotus II Philopator was deposed in 30 BC, although he was restored to power between 20 BC and 17 AD.[52]
Parts of Cilicia were given to Antiochus IV of Commagene by Caligula, who incorporated the rest of it into Syria.[52]
A united province of Cilicia consisting of both Rugged and Plain Cilicia with Tarsus as capital was re-established in 72 AD by Vespasian.[46][52][53]
During the early 2nd century AD, 39 cities of Cilicia issued coins.[46]
In 194 AD, Septimius Severus defeated Pescennius Niger at the Cilician Gates.[52] Under the Severan dynasty, during the late 2nd to early 3rd centuries AD, the city of Anazarbus, which was made into a metropolis, became a rival of Tarsus.[53]
In 259 or 260, the Persian Sasanian king of kings Shapur I defeated the Roman Emperor Valerian, whose army included Cilician soldiers. After Valerian's defeat, the Sasanian forces burnt and sacked several cities in Syria, Cilicia (Middle Persian: 𐭪𐭫𐭪𐭩𐭠𐭩) and Cappadocia, and devastated large parts of Cilicia.[47][52]
Under Diocletian's reforms, Cilicia was split into Cilicia Prima, Cilicia Secunda which included the northwestern part of Syria now known as Hatay, and a province named Isauria with its capital at Seleucia which included Rugged Cilicia.[52]
Cilicia had numerous Christian communities and is mentioned six times in the Book of Acts and once in the Epistle to the Galatians (1:21).[54] After Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire in the 4th century, Cilicia was included in the territories of the patriarchate of Antioch.[55] The region was divided into two civil and ecclesiastical provinces: Cilicia Prima, with a metropolitan diocese at Tarsus and suffragan dioceses for Pompeiopolis, Sebaste, Augusta, Corycus, Adana, Mallus and Zephyrium; and Cilicia Secunda, with a metropolitan diocese at Anazarbus and suffragan dioceses for Mopsuestia, Aegae, Epiphania, Irenopolis, Flavias, Castabala, Alexandria, Citidiopolis and Rhosus. Bishops from the various dioceses of Cilicia were well represented at the First Council of Nicaea in 325 and at the later ecumenical councils.[56]
In 400, Theodosius I divided Plain Cilicia into the provinces of Cilicia Prima, headquartered at Tarsus, and Cilicia Secunda, whose capital was Anazarbus.[57][53]
The Christian Church in Cilicia was under the authority of the Patriarch of Antioch.[57]
Cilicia remained prosperous, due to which several, largely ecclesiastical, construction works were undertaken there.[57]
From the middle of the 7th century, Cilicia became more and more close to the border between the Byzantine Empire and the Caliphate, resulting in the depopulation of the region.[57]
Early Islamic period
[edit]In the 7th century Cilicia was invaded by the Muslim Arabs.[58] The area was for some time an embattled no-man's land. The Umayyad Caliphate conquered Cilicia around c. 700.[57] Under the Abbasid Caliphate, Cilicia was resettled and transformed into a fortified frontier zone (thughur).[59] Tarsus, re-built in 787/788, quickly became the largest settlement in the region and the Arabs' most important base in their raids across the Taurus Mountains into Byzantine-held Anatolia.[citation needed] Fortified settlements such as Ḥiṣn al-Tīnāt (identified with the Tüpraş Field near Kinet Höyük) were not only military posts but also played economic roles, showing that parts of coastal Cilicia functioned not merely as a border zone.[59]
In medieval Arabic Cilicia was known as Ath-Thugur As-Shamiyya meaning "Levantine outskirts".
The Muslims held the country until it was reoccupied by the Emperor Nicephorus II in 965.[19][57] During the Byzantine resettlement of Cilicia, many Armenians migrated to Cilicia, where they founded in 1071 the kingdom of Lesser Armenia.[57]
Armenian Cilicia and the Crusades
[edit]During the time of the First Crusade, the area was controlled by the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia. The Seljuk Turkish invasions of Armenia were followed by an exodus of Armenians migrating westward into the Byzantine Empire, and in 1080 Ruben, a relative of the last king of Ani, founded in the heart of the Cilician Taurus a small principality which gradually expanded into the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia. This Christian state, surrounded by Muslim states hostile to its existence, had a stormy history of about 300 years, giving valuable support to the Crusaders, and trading with the great commercial cities of Italy.[19]
It prospered for three centuries due to the vast network of fortifications which secured all the major roads as well as the three principal harbours at Ayas, Koŕikos, and Mopsuestia.[60] Through their complex alliances with the Crusader states, the Armenian barons and kings often invited Crusaders to maintain castles in and along the borders of the Kingdom, including Bagras, Trapessac, T‛il Hamtun, Harunia, Selefkia, Amouda, and Sarvandikar.
